steps.note: Scripted run for this picture: on loop 1 you type nothing, on loop 2 you press j, on loop 3 you press q. The box called key is empty for now.
count starts at 0. It will count how many times the loop goes round.
for (;;) has no condition, so it loops forever. Only break gets us out. Watch the lane: it keeps moving the whole time.
Loop 1 begins. Start by assuming no key: key = 0.
_kbhit() glances at the letterbox. Nothing there, so it answers 0 straight away and the while loop is skipped.
key is 0, not 'q', so we stay in the loop.
count goes up on every loop, whether or not you touched the keyboard. The lane moves one step.
key is 0, so there is nothing to print this time.
Loop 2. key goes back to 0. While we weren't looking, you pressed j and it landed in the letterbox.
_kbhit() peeks and sees a key waiting, so it answers 1 and the loop body runs.
_getch() takes the waiting key out of the letterbox and puts it in key. No Enter needed.
Peek again. The letterbox is empty now, so _kbhit() says 0 and the while loop ends.
key is 'j', not 'q', so no break.
count becomes 2. The lane moves another step.
key is not 0, so this time there is something to print.
printf shows which key arrived and on which loop.
Loop 3. key resets to 0, and you press q.
A key is waiting, so _kbhit() says 1.
_getch() takes the q.
Letterbox empty again, so the while loop ends.
key is 'q'. This is true.
break jumps out of the forever loop.
The program ends. count stopped at 2 because loop 3 left before count++.
Scripted for this picture: we watch frames 1 and 2, skip ahead through 3 to 29, then see frame 30. This line asks windows.h to leave out the rarely used parts.
windows.h is where Sleep lives. Capital S.
One named number for the frame length: 33 milliseconds. 1000 divided by 33 is about 30 frames a second.
frame is an int that will count the frames. The film strip on top has 30 slots, all empty.
The loop starts at frame 1 and will run while frame is 30 or less.
Do the frame's work. Here that is one printf. A bright block appears in the CPU bar: it only takes a moment.
Sleep(33) hands the CPU back to Windows. The clock fills for about 33 ms while other programs get a turn.
frame goes to 2, still 30 or less, so round again.
Frame 2: a little work, then a print.
Sleep again. About 33 ms each time, never exact: Windows wakes you on its next timer tick.
Frames 3 to 29 repeat the same three beats: print, sleep, next. We fast-forward through them.

steps.note: Frame 30, the last one. The strip is full once this prints.
The last sleep.
frame becomes 31, which is more than 30, so the loop is over.
After about a second of sleeping, we say we are done.
The program ends. 30 frames took roughly one second.
score is a box that will hold the number we draw.
score starts at 11, and 11 is 9 or more, so the loop runs.
printf hands \r and 'score 11' to stdout. Some terminals hold it until a newline, so fflush makes sure it shows.
fflush pushes the buffer out. The cursor is already at column 0, so \r changes nothing yet and 'score 11' appears.
score goes down to 10. Still 9 or more, so go again.
Same again: \r, then 'score 10', waiting in the buffer.
This time \r snaps the cursor back to column 0. There is no newline, so 'score 10' types right over 'score 11'.
score is 9. Still 9 or more, so one more.
\r and 'score 9' go into the buffer.
'score 9' is one character shorter, so it doesn't cover the 0 from 'score 10'. That 0 is left behind and the line reads score 90.
score drops to 8. 8 is not 9 or more, so the loop ends.
Only now do we print a newline. The cursor drops to the next line so the shell prompt doesn't land on top of the score.
Done. A real game would pad or clear the line so nothing is left behind.
LANE_LEN is a text replacement: wherever the code says LANE_LEN, the compiler sees 12.
PLAYER_COL is 2: the player stands in slot 2.
Make the frame buffer: 13 slots, 12 for the lane and one spare for the \0 that ends a string. They hold leftover junk (?) for now.
obs_col is the obstacle's column: 8.
memset paints the 12 lane slots with dots. That's the blank road.
The \0 goes in the spare slot so printf knows where the string stops.
Stamp an obstacle: slot 8 becomes #. It happens in memory, so nothing shows yet.
Stamp the player on top: slot 2 becomes A. Later stamps cover earlier ones, so if both wanted a slot the player would win.
One printf rolls the finished row out to the screen all at once. No half-painted frame.
Done. The row is on screen exactly as it was painted backstage.
A pretend keyboard stands in for _kbhit: one key per frame. A d is the third key (frame 2). The picture's strip shows them.
pos starts at 0, the left of the lane.
The heartbeat starts. frame is 0.
1. Input: read this frame's key. keys[0] is '.', so no key.
2. Update: ducking is 1 only if the key is 'd'. '.' is not, so ducking is 0.
Still update: the runner moves one step. pos is 1.
3. Render: show the result.
4. Wait: the real game sleeps here, then the loop goes round again.
frame++ makes frame 1. 1 < 5, so round again.
Frame 1, input: keys[1] is '.', no key again.
Update: not 'd', so ducking is 0.
pos goes to 2.
Render.
Wait.
frame++ makes frame 2. 2 < 5, so round again.
Frame 2, input: keys[2] is 'd'. A key press!
Update: the key is 'd', so (key == 'd') is 1 and the runner ducks.
pos goes to 3. The runner moves while ducked.
Render: ducking 1 is printed.
Wait.
Frames 3 and 4 go round the same four beats fast. The d is gone, so ducking drops back to 0 and the runner stands up again.
steps.out:
frame 3: pos 4 ducking 0
frame 4: pos 5 ducking 0

steps.note: The loop is done after five frames. Every game is this same heartbeat.
obs is an array of four bays. We haven't put anything in them yet, so they hold junk (?).
score starts at 0.
The loop visits each bay and writes -1. Every bay gets a cone: -1 means free.
Frame 0 begins.
The inner loop walks over the bays. Every one holds -1, so the if skips them all. Nothing moves.
0 % 2 is 0, so this is a spawn frame.
Search for the first free bay. Bay 0 holds -1, so this is the one.
A car enters bay 0. The number 2 is its column.
break stops the search. Without it, every free bay would get a car.
Frame 1. Bay 0 holds a car, so it moves one column toward the player: 2 becomes 1. The empty bays are skipped. 1 is not below 0, and frame 1 is odd, so no new car.
Frame 2. The car moves again: 1 becomes 0. 0 is not below 0, so it stays on the road.
Frame 2 is even, so another car spawns.
Search for a free bay. Bay 0 is busy, so skip it. Bay 1 has a cone: take it.
A new car enters bay 1.
break again, so only one bay is used.
Frame 3. Bay 0's car moves: 0 minus 1 is -1. It has gone past the player.
Below column 0 means dodged. -1 is less than 0, so the if is true.
Put the bay back to -1. Here it already is -1, but this line is what frees any bay that goes below 0.
One obstacle dodged: score goes to 1.
The inner loop reaches bay 1: its car moves from 2 to 1.
Frame 4. Bay 1's car moves: 1 becomes 0. Frame 4 is even, so a spawn is coming.
Search for a free bay. Bay 0 holds a cone again, so a new car can take it.
A car enters bay 0, then break stops the search.
After five frames the bays hold 2, 0, -1, -1 and the score is 1.
Done. No bay was ever built or demolished, only the numbers changed.
An enum gives the three states names. Underneath they are the numbers 0, 1 and 2. The picture shows each state as a box.
A pretend keyboard, one key per frame. '.' means no key. The picture shows the keys along the top.
The game starts on the menu. This one variable is the whole machine's memory.
Frame 0: the key is '.', so no key.
switch looks at state and jumps to the case that matches. Only the MENU rules run this frame.
The menu only wants a key press, and '.' means none. So state stays MENU.
Print the state number.
Frame 1: the key is 'x'.
A key press! The menu hands over: state becomes STATE_PLAYING.
Print the state number.
Frame 2: no key.
While playing, only 'h' matters. Not an h, so nothing changes.
Print the state number.
Frame 3: the key is 'h', a hit.
An h ends the run: state becomes STATE_GAME_OVER.
Print the state number.
Frame 4: the key is 'x'.
Game over only listens for 'r'. An x does nothing, so state stays put.
Print the state number.
Frame 5: the key is 'r'.
An r restarts: state goes back to STATE_PLAYING.
Print the state number.
The loop ends after six frames. The state followed the keys, one rule at a time.
In main we make a Runner. It is one card holding a score and a frame. Both are junk (?) for now.
score starts at 0.
frame starts at 0.
We call runner_update and pass &r, the address of the card. Its pointer r now points at the real Runner.
This is a normal pointer: runner_update can read and change whatever it points at. It holds a key.
r->score++ changes the real score in main, because r points at it. score is 1.
The frame is changed the same way: 1.
A second call. The same pointer reaches the same card.
score becomes 2.
frame becomes 2.
Now runner_render gets &r. A normal pointer converts to a read-only one automatically, so this is allowed.
const Runner* means: r points at a Runner I'm not allowed to change. It is a visitor's pass: look, but don't touch. Writing through it would stop the program building.
Reading is fine. printf only looks at score and frame.
Done. render only read the card, so it still says score 2, frame 2.

Not a program run: this shows what the linker does with the header. main.c and runner.c each start with #include "runner.h". An include is copy and paste, so both files get their own copy of every line. The console shows linker messages, not program output.
#pragma once stops the header being pasted twice into one file. It doesn't help across two files: each .c file still gets one copy.
A #define makes no code of its own. It is a text replacement, so two copies are harmless.
A typedef only describes a shape. It makes nothing in memory, so it is safe in a header.
This is the problem. It creates a variable. Each file compiles into an .obj, and each .obj now owns its own best_score.
A prototype is a promise: this function exists somewhere. Any number of files can say it. This is what headers are for.
The linker joins the .obj files and finds best_score defined in both. It can't pick one, so it refuses.
steps.out:
runner.obj : error LNK2005: _best_score already defined in main.obj
main.exe : fatal error LNK1169: one or more multiply defined symbols found

steps.note: The fix. In the header, write extern int best_score; which only says best_score exists somewhere. Then define it once, in runner.c: int best_score = 0;. Now there is exactly one.
